analysis.executiveSummary:
Oddzilla is a real-money esports sportsbook with a generally mature security posture — apply-once settlement, hash-chained audit logs, signer isolation, 4-eyes withdrawals, and a prior 6-PR audit pass are all in place — but this round surfaces four HIGH-severity issues that each individually undermine a load-bearing control, plus systemic gaps in rate-limiting and concurrency safety. The single most urgent is the deposit-attribution-theft primitive: POST /wallet/addresses lets any bettor claim an arbitrary sending address with zero ownership proof (first-writer-wins), so registering a public CEX hot-wallet address steals every subsequent exchange-sourced deposit. It is a wired, shipping pre-launch feature and must be gated before ETH_RPC_URL is populated. Equally critical is the secrets-handling regression: docker-compose injects the full .env (JWT_SECRET, REFRESH_COOKIE_SECRET, HD_MASTER_MNEMONIC, POSTGRES_PASSWORD) into the internet-facing Next.js web replicas via `env_file: .env`, directly re-enabling the HS256 admin-token forgery the codebase explicitly designed around — and deploy.sh re-exposes the same crown-jewel mnemonic via /proc/<pid>/environ during every migration deploy.

Two recurring themes dominate the findings. First, RATE-LIMITING is absent on entire route families: ws-gateway (no maxPayload → single-frame OOM in a 256 MiB container; no per-IP cap → one host monopolizes 5000 slots), anonymous /catalog/search (leading-wildcard ILIKE seq-scans that exhaust the 10-connection pool), self-service withdrawals, zillapass tracking, and the public mail-receiver SMTP — all reachable without authentication or with a cheap authenticated loop, against a single small Postgres pool. Second, CONCURRENCY: the RiskZilla solvency gate is a read-committed TOCTOU evaluated entirely from non-locking SELECTs, so concurrent placements by different bettors can collectively breach both the bank_limit (solvency ceiling) and per-match liability caps; relatedly, bet-delay rejections leak open_liability_micro (fail-safe but availability-degrading drift).

The headline risk profile is fund loss (deposit theft, admin-token forgery, mnemonic exposure) and availability (multiple trivial DoS vectors saturating the shared DB pool / OOMing single-process services). Lower-severity findings cluster around incomplete kill-switches (block doesn't revoke sessions), dormant tamper-evidence (audit-chain verifier never runs automatically), and gameable loyalty/leaderboard surfaces (AI-account leakage, self-farmable inspiration counters) that become real-money issues once the planned Oz redemption path ships. Net: solid foundations, but the deposit-whitelist, the compose secret injection, and the DoS surface are launch-blocking.
topPriorities: Gate POST /wallet/addresses behind cryptographic ownership proof (EIP-191/SIWE) and blocklist CEX hot-wallet addresses before ETH_RPC_URL is populated — close the deposit-attribution-theft primitive

Stop injecting .env into the web containers: replace `env_file: .env` on the *web-base anchor with an explicit web-scoped env block excluding JWT_SECRET/REFRESH_COOKIE_SECRET/HD_MASTER_MNEMONIC/POSTGRES_PASSWORD — re-close the HS256 admin-token forgery path
Set an explicit small maxPayload (e.g. 16 KiB) on the ws-gateway WebSocketServer to stop anonymous single-frame OOM of the 256 MiB container
Serialize the RiskZilla bank-state + per-match liability gates with a pg_advisory_xact_lock so concurrent cross-user placements cannot breach bank_limit / match-liability caps
Replace `set -a; . .env; set +a` in deploy.sh with a targeted DATABASE_URL read so HD_MASTER_MNEMONIC stops appearing in deploy child-process /proc/<pid>/environ

Add per-IP rate limits to anonymous /catalog/search and the catalog list endpoints (and per-IP connection caps + inbound token bucket on ws-gateway) to protect the 10-connection DB pool and gateway from saturation
Revoke all sessions + prime the Redis revoke cache on user block / role change in PATCH /admin/users/:id so the kill switch is immediate
Cap the inbound-email References chain (and add a webhook rate limit) to stop the unbounded sequential-query amplification DoS reachable via the public MX
coverageGaps: Settlement Go service internals — the apply-once 5-tuple, payout math edge cases, and rollback/re-settle generation-suffix ledger refs were referenced but not deeply re-audited this pass; verify no concurrency or replay gap mirrors the RiskZilla TOCTOU
wallet-watcher reorg-safety and confirmation-tick logic beyond the attribution path (block_hash verification, orphaned-state transitions, multi-Transfer log_index collisions)
Specifier-hash byte-identity across the three implementations (TS + 2 Go) against the golden fixture — a divergence silently breaks settlement matching but was not re-verified here
ws-gateway per-subscriber bettor-odds-adjustment cache + Redis invalidation channel for cross-user data leakage or stale-price exploitation
Caddy edge configuration depth — only /api/* has a body cap and X-Forwarded-For; /ws and /webhooks/* lack equivalent edge protections; review whether other unprotected paths exist
The full admin route surface for additional missing session/role re-checks (the block-revocation gap suggests other admin mutations may also trust the frozen 15-min role claim)
BetBuilder / OBB gRPC placement + settlement path (currently env-gated off) for the same TOCTOU and apply-once guarantees once enabled
Pre-launch exit gates explicitly still open per CLAUDE.md: KYC, daily wallet reconciliation, off-host encrypted backup rsync, and production monitoring/alerting wiring

Oz loyalty ledger before the first redemption/spend path lands — the self-farmable inspiration counters become a mint-money primitive at that point and the whole earn surface needs anti-sybil review then

findings.title: Blocking a user (and role changes) does not revoke active sessions — authenticated access persists up to the 15-min access-token lifetime
findings.description: When an admin sets a user's status to 'blocked' (or changes their role) via PATCH /admin/users/:id, the handler updates users.status (services/api/src/modules/admin/users.ts:319-323, 350-362) and writes an audit row, but it never revokes the user's sessions. The session-revocation cache and the auth preHandler key on sessions.revokedAt only — they never consult users.status or users.role (services/api/src/plugins/auth.ts:80-103). A previously-issued access JWT therefore stays valid for its full lifetime (JWT_ACCESS_TTL_SECONDS, default 900s = 15 min). The access token also carries a frozen `role` claim (packages/auth/src/jwt.ts:17-30; minted from the user row at services/api/src/modules/auth/service.ts:762-772), so a demotion from admin→user likewise leaves the old admin role honoured by requireRole() for up to 15 minutes. Refresh is correctly gated (svc.refresh checks user.status==='blocked' at service.ts:473), so the blocked user cannot extend the window past one access-token expiry — but the existing token keeps working. Impact is bounded because the two money-moving endpoints independently re-read users.status at request time inside their transaction (wallet withdrawals: services/api/src/modules/wallet/routes.ts:205-213; bet placement: services/api/src/modules/bets/service.ts:313-325), so a blocked user cannot place bets or request withdrawals. The residual exposure is read endpoints (/auth/me, /wallet balances, ticket history) and low-value mutations (profile edits, support chat, community posts/analyses, devices) staying accessible for ≤15 min after the operator hits the emergency-block button, plus the admin-role-demotion staleness window for any /admin/** action.
findings.exploitScenario: Fraud/AML team detects an account abusing the platform and blocks it. For up to 15 minutes the blocked account continues to hold a valid session: it can read its own data, post in community/support, and (for a demoted-not-blocked admin) continue invoking /admin/** routes that the JWT's stale role still satisfies. The block is intended as an immediate kill switch, but it is not.
findings.recommendation: On status change to a non-active value (and on any role change) in PATCH /admin/users/:id, revoke every active session for the target user in the same transaction and prime the Redis revoke cache — reuse the existing AuthService.revokeAllSessions() pattern (services/api/src/modules/auth/service.ts:527-534) which already does `UPDATE sessions SET revoked_at = now() WHERE user_id=? AND revoked_at IS NULL` plus cacheRevoked() per session. Additionally, consider having the auth preHandler treat status='blocked' as non-authenticated (a small extra users.status read, or fold status into the cached session-status value) so the kill switch is immediate regardless of which endpoint is hit.

findings.title: Bet-delay rejection does not release RiskZilla open_liability_micro (recoverable bookkeeping drift)
findings.description: At placement, RiskzillaEngine.commitAccepted() unconditionally bumps riskzilla_bank_state.open_liability_micro by the ticket's full potential_payout for every accepted ticket — INCLUDING tickets put into status='pending_delay' (placement happens before the bet-delay window). When the bet-delay worker later rejects such a ticket (odds_drift_exceeded / market_suspended / outcome_inactive / no_current_price), store.RejectAndRefund() flips the ticket to 'rejected', unlocks the stake, and writes a bet_refund ledger row, but it never decrements open_liability_micro. The settlement-side decrement (UpdateRiskzillaBankOnSettle) only fires on settle/cancel/rollback for accepted tickets that actually reach settlement, so a rejected ticket's potential_payout stays permanently counted as open exposure. This is fail-SAFE: a too-high open_liability makes the bank gate (userBalances + openLiability + bet > bankLimit in engine.ts:596) MORE conservative, rejecting bets it would otherwise accept — it never lets unbacked liability through. It self-heals on POST /admin/riskzilla/bank/recompute (admin/riskzilla/bank.ts:322-328 sums only status IN ('accepted','pending_delay')). Under sustained live-bet drift rejection, the counter monotonically inflates and can eventually start rejecting legitimate bets with bank_limit_exceeded until an operator recomputes.
findings.exploitScenario: A bettor (or organic live-bet churn) repeatedly places live single/combo bets that the bet-delay worker rejects on odds drift. Each rejection leaks the ticket's potential_payout into open_liability_micro. Over enough rejections the cached counter grows large enough that genuine bets from any USDC bettor start failing with bank_limit_exceeded, a denial-of-service on bet acceptance until an operator runs /admin/riskzilla/bank/recompute. No funds are lost or over-credited; the impact is gate over-tightening / availability.
findings.recommendation: In RejectAndRefund (and any path that takes a ticket from pending_delay/accepted to rejected outside settlement), decrement riskzilla_bank_state.open_liability_micro by the ticket's potential_payout_micro for USDC tickets — mirroring UpdateRiskzillaBankOnSettle's GREATEST(0, open_liability_micro - $1) guard so it can't underflow. Pass potential_payout through PendingTicket (already loaded) into RejectAndRefund.

findings.title: Deposit attribution theft: linked sending-address whitelist accepts any address with no ownership proof (first-writer-wins)
findings.description: POST /wallet/addresses lets any authenticated bettor register an arbitrary ERC20 `from` address as 'their' sending wallet with zero proof of control (no signature challenge, no micro-deposit verification). The only constraints are the regex format check and a global UNIQUE (network, address) (migration 0035_user_wallet_addresses.sql:27; schema deposits.ts:199), which makes registration strictly first-writer-wins. The wallet-watcher's DiscoverIncoming (services/wallet-watcher/internal/ethereum/scanner.go:231-266) scans every USDC Transfer TO the shared receive address and attributes each to a user purely via store.LookupUserByWalletAddress(from) (store.go:78-92) against this unproven whitelist, then auto-creates a `confirming` deposit_intent and credits it (processor.go credit path -> store.CreditIntent). The wallet/routes.ts header comment (lines 11-15) claims the team removed the user-facing 'paste your tx hash' route specifically because 'exposing a self-claim endpoint would let any attacker on Etherscan grab another user's tx hash and steal their deposit' — but the whitelist-registration channel reintroduces an equivalent (and broader) theft primitive: instead of needing a specific tx hash, the attacker only needs to know an address a victim will send FROM. Critically, deposits funded by a centralized exchange withdrawal (Coinbase/Binance/etc., the most common way a retail bettor moves USDC) originate from the exchange's SHARED hot-wallet address, which is public knowledge. An attacker who registers a major CEX hot-wallet address first will have EVERY subsequent CEX-sourced deposit from that hot wallet auto-credited to the attacker's account, not the real depositor's — a mass-attribution-theft / wrong-credit vector. There is no compensating control anywhere in the codebase (grep for verifyMessage/personal_sign/challenge/nonce/proof in wallet module returns nothing).
findings.exploitScenario: Attacker registers Binance's well-known USDC hot-wallet address (public on Etherscan) via POST /wallet/addresses on their own account; the UNIQUE constraint means they own that mapping first. Victim withdraws 500 USDC from Binance to Oddzilla's shared receive address. wallet-watcher's DiscoverIncoming sees the Transfer, looks up the `from` (Binance hot wallet) -> attacker, inserts a `confirming` deposit_intent for the attacker, counts confirmations, and CreditIntent credits 500 USDC to the attacker's wallet. The victim's deposit never appears in their account; the attacker withdraws the stolen balance. The same attack scales to every CEX-sourced deposit from that hot wallet until the address is unregistered.
findings.recommendation: Require cryptographic proof of control before a `from` address can be used for auto-attribution: issue a per-user nonce and require an EIP-191 personal_sign / SIWE signature over it, recover the signer with ethers.verifyMessage, and only insert when it matches. Additionally, explicitly blocklist known CEX/custodial hot-wallet addresses from the whitelist (shared-custody addresses can never prove single-user ownership). Treat the linked-wallet whitelist as a convenience layer ONLY for self-custodial sends with a proven signature; route everything else (including all CEX-sourced deposits) to admin review at /admin/deposits rather than auto-crediting. As defense in depth, when DiscoverIncoming attributes a Transfer, flag/hold rather than auto-credit when the `from` looks like a high-volume contract/exchange address.

findings.title: Inbound email References header triggers unbounded sequential DB queries inside one transaction (amplification DoS)
findings.category: Denial of Service / untrusted input amplification
findings.location: services/api/src/modules/email/inbound/threading.ts:130-133 (loop); resolveOrCreateThread invoked inside the transaction at services/api/src/modules/email/inbound/routes.ts:142-183; chain parsed unbounded at threading.ts:36-44
findings.description: The inbound-mail webhook resolves which thread a message belongs to by walking the RFC 5322 References chain. `parseReferencesChain` (threading.ts:36-44) extracts EVERY `<...>` id from the References header with no length cap, and `resolveOrCreateThread` (threading.ts:130-133) loops over the entire chain newest-to-oldest, issuing TWO sequential DB queries per id (`findThreadByReferencedMessageId` queries both emailOutbox and emailInbound at threading.ts:65-77). This whole walk runs inside `app.db.transaction(...)` (routes.ts:142). The References value rides in the `headers` multipart field, which is bounded only by the multipart `fieldSize: 1 MiB` limit (routes.ts:62-67). A 1 MiB header block of minimal fake ids (`<a@b>` ≈ 5 bytes) yields ~200,000 ids → ~400,000 sequential round-trips inside a single long-lived transaction. Crucially this is reachable WITHOUT knowing the webhook secret: the self-hosted mail-receiver (services/mail-receiver) is a public SMTP listener on port 25 that accepts mail for the storefront domain from anyone (no SPF/DKIM/auth, main.go:171-188) and forwards it to this webhook with the shared secret it holds (relay.go:78-86). So any external party can drive this by sending one crafted email to anything@oddzilla.cc. The stored `referencesChain.join(' ')` (routes.ts:157) and the up-to-1 MiB text/html body fields are also persisted, so each such message also writes multi-MiB rows.
findings.exploitScenario: An attacker sends a single email to support@oddzilla.cc (or any address @oddzilla.cc) with a ~1 MiB References header full of non-matching message-ids. mail-receiver accepts it (recipient is on-domain) and POSTs to /webhooks/sendgrid-inbound/<secret>. The webhook opens a DB transaction and performs hundreds of thousands of sequential SELECTs against email_outbox + email_inbound, holding the transaction open for minutes and saturating the single Postgres connection pool shared with the live storefront/API. Repeating a few of these in parallel degrades or stalls all DB-backed traffic (bets, wallet, auth) on the box.
findings.recommendation: Cap the References chain before walking it (e.g. take only the last 10-20 ids — RFC reply chains are short; the most-recent ancestors are all that matter) and/or resolve the chain with a single `WHERE message_id = ANY($1)`/`IN` query instead of N sequential round-trips. Also bound `parseReferencesChain` output length and the persisted `referencesChain` string. Independently, add a rate limit to the inbound webhook route (it currently states 'No rate limit', routes.ts:84-86) and to the mail-receiver SMTP backend, since the public MX makes this endpoint reachable by unauthenticated senders rather than only by a trusted SendGrid.

findings.description: mail-receiver is an unauthenticated public SMTP server (port 25) that accepts mail for the storefront domain from any sender (no SPF/DKIM/DMARC, by design per the header comment main.go:19-26). Each accepted message (up to 8 MiB, main.go:70) is forwarded to the api webhook, which inserts a row into email_inbound storing the full text and html bodies inline plus the raw header block (routes.ts:151-169), and creates a fresh email_threads row whenever threading finds no match (threading.ts:142-153). There is no connection cap, no per-source rate limit, and no overall inbound volume cap. An attacker can send a high volume of large emails to arbitrary local-parts @oddzilla.cc, each creating a new thread + multi-MiB inbound row, growing the Postgres data directory unbounded. Given the box's documented prior disk-full incidents that took postgres down for days, unbounded inbound-mail storage is a concrete operational risk.
findings.exploitScenario: An attacker loops sending ~8 MiB emails with unique subjects to random addresses @oddzilla.cc. Each is stored as a new email_threads + email_inbound row with full bodies. Sustained, this fills the data volume (which co-locates postgres, the api, and Go workers) and induces a disk-full outage of the entire stack.
findings.recommendation: Add a per-remote-IP connection/message rate limit in the SMTP backend (main.go), reject senders that fail a basic SPF/DMARC check or at least throttle them, and add a retention/size policy on email_inbound + email_threads (cap inbound table size, prune old un-threaded junk). Consider only accepting mail for a small allowlist of real local-parts (support@, noreply-bounces@, etc.) rather than any address ending in @domain (main.go:179).

findings.title: JWT_SECRET and REFRESH_COOKIE_SECRET injected into the Next.js web containers via `env_file: .env`, re-enabling token forgery the design explicitly removed
findings.description:
The web tier was deliberately decoupled from JWT verification so a web RCE cannot mint tokens. apps/web/src/lib/auth.ts documents this directly: "We deliberately do NOT verify access tokens locally here — that would require sharing JWT_SECRET with the web container and turn a web RCE into the ability to mint admin tokens. Instead every session check goes through the API's /auth/me endpoint." CLAUDE.md echoes it: "Web container no longer carries JWT_SECRET." No web-tier code calls `loadAuthEnv()` (grep confirms only apps/web/src/lib/auth.ts matches JWT_SECRET, and it only contains the comment).

But the `*web-base` anchor (docker-compose.yml line 103) sets `env_file: .env`, and web1/web2/web3 all inherit it (`<<: *web-base`). The `.env` file holds `JWT_SECRET` and `REFRESH_COOKIE_SECRET` (.env.example lines 43-44; CLAUDE.md "Local secrets that exist"). Compose injects both into every web container's `process.env` regardless of whether the code reads them. Access tokens are signed with HS256 (packages/auth/src/jwt.ts:23 — `alg: "HS256"`), a symmetric algorithm, so possession of JWT_SECRET is sufficient to FORGE valid tokens, not just verify them. The web containers are the primary internet-facing SSR surface (rich attack surface: SSR, image/iframe proxies, user-controlled fetches), making this the exact scenario the auth.ts comment claims is foreclosed. REFRESH_COOKIE_SECRET (cookie signing) and ODDIN_TOKEN, EMAIL_PROVIDER_TOKEN, DISIR_BRAND_TOKEN, POSTGRES_PASSWORD etc. are likewise all injected into web.
findings.exploitScenario: An attacker gains code execution or an arbitrary-read in one of the three Next.js SSR replicas (a common, large attack surface). They read `process.env.JWT_SECRET` and locally forge an access JWT with `{sub: <any user id>, role: "admin", sid: <any>}`, `aud=oddzilla-api`, signed HS256 with the stolen secret. Presenting this JWT as the `oddzilla_access` cookie to the API authenticates them as an admin on sadmin.oddzilla.cc, granting access to every /admin/* route (user management, balance adjustments, withdrawals). The Redis session-revocation cache doesn't help because a forged sid simply isn't marked revoked. The documented containment ("a compromised web server cannot forge a valid token") is void.
findings.recommendation: Remove `env_file: .env` from the `*web-base` anchor and provide the web containers only the keys they actually need (PORT, HOSTNAME, ADMIN_HOST, REPLICA_NAME, FRONTEND_HOST, INTERNAL_API_URL, NEXT_PUBLIC_* — all already listed inline). Use an explicit `environment:` block (like metrics-collector/mail-receiver) or a web-scoped env file that excludes JWT_SECRET, REFRESH_COOKIE_SECRET, HD_MASTER_MNEMONIC, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, ODDIN_TOKEN, and all provider tokens. Verify post-fix with `docker compose exec web1 env | grep -E 'JWT_SECRET|REFRESH_COOKIE|HD_MASTER|POSTGRES_PASSWORD'` returning nothing.

findings.title: Public /community/leaderboard surfaces AI seed accounts — missing the is_ai exclusion every other community surface enforces
findings.location: services/api/src/modules/community/leaderboard.ts:249-261 (FROM users u ... WHERE clause has no u.is_ai = false / nickname filter)
findings.description:
Decision D2 in CLAUDE.md mandates that AI seed accounts (`users.is_ai = true`) are internal-only and excluded from public-facing surfaces, and the SEC-C1 audit produced a shared visibility helper (services/api/src/modules/community/visibility.ts) carrying `tickets_public = true AND nickname IS NOT NULL AND is_ai = false`. Every other community read funnels through it: feed (PUBLIC_AUTHOR_SQL), profile/tickets (isPubliclyVisibleAuthor), projection, achievements, analyses, competitions, and notifications all gate on `is_ai = false`.

The public, anonymous `GET /community/leaderboard` does NOT. Its main query (lines 249-261) is `FROM users u LEFT JOIN oz_window o ... LEFT JOIN analysis_stats s ... WHERE (o.user_id IS NOT NULL OR s.user_id IS NOT NULL)` with no `u.is_ai = false` predicate and no `u.nickname IS NOT NULL` predicate. Any AI seed account that has an oz_ledger row or a published analysis is ranked and returned with its nickname + avatar + stats on the public Top Authors board, contradicting the documented invariant. (The `is_ai` column value itself is not serialized, so this is data-surface leakage of seeded rows, not a secret leak; severity is correspondingly low.) The missing `nickname IS NOT NULL` filter also means `RawLeaderboardRow.nickname` (typed non-null) can serialize a literal null for an admin-credited user with no nickname.
findings.exploitScenario: A user opens the Community leaderboard (or scrapes GET /community/leaderboard, 60/min/IP). Fabricated AI seed bettors that have received Oz credits or published analyses appear interleaved with real users in the public ranking, presenting bot-generated activity as genuine community standing — the exact outcome Decision D2 and the SEC-C1 fix were meant to prevent. No fund loss, but it undermines the integrity guarantee and may mislead bettors about real activity.
findings.recommendation: Route the leaderboard query through the same visibility predicate as the rest of the module: add `u.is_ai = false` (and `u.nickname IS NOT NULL`) to the WHERE clause, e.g. reuse `PUBLIC_AUTHOR_SQL` (which uses the `u` alias already present here) or append the conditions explicitly. This keeps the leaderboard in lockstep with the documented SEC-C1 invariant and the other community surfaces.

The `analysis_stats` CTE (lines 184-222) and `oz_window` CTE (178-183) also omit any is_ai filter.

findings.title: RiskZilla bank-limit (solvency) gate is a read-committed TOCTOU — concurrent placements by different bettors can collectively exceed bank_limit_micro
findings.description: The bet placement transaction (services/api/src/modules/bets/service.ts, this.db.transaction at line 292) acquires FOR UPDATE only on the placing user's own users row (line 320) and their own wallets row (line 332). The RiskZilla solvency gate, however, is evaluated entirely from NON-LOCKING SELECTs: engine.ts line 265-270 reads riskzilla_bank_state (bank_limit_micro, open_liability_micro) with a plain SELECT, and line 286-290 reads SUM(balance_micro - locked_micro) over all USDC wallets — neither uses FOR UPDATE. The gate at line 596 (`userBalances + openLiability + bankIncremental > bankLimit`) is the operator's hard solvency check against real crypto cash (explicitly described that way at line 586-594). commitAccepted() then increments open_liability_micro AFTER the decision (line 630-635), and its own header comment (line 199) states the evaluation is 'Pure read; safe to call ... without write-locking RiskZilla rows.' The DB runs at the default READ COMMITTED isolation (packages/db/src/index.ts createDb sets no isolation level; no SERIALIZABLE/REPEATABLE READ anywhere). Two placement transactions by DIFFERENT users do not share any lock during evaluate(), so each reads the same open_liability/balances snapshot, each independently passes the bank gate, and each then increments the counter. The atomic `+= incremental` UPDATE keeps the counter value itself correct, but the gate decisions were both made on stale pre-increment data — classic write-skew. (A SINGLE user racing themselves IS serialized by the per-user users-row FOR UPDATE, so this is specifically a cross-user exposure on the shared bank_state + wallet-sum aggregates.) Result: committed open liability can exceed bank_limit_micro, defeating the solvency ceiling that protects the operator from owing more on simultaneous wins than the bank physically holds.
findings.exploitScenario: Operator sets bank_limit_micro = 10,000 USDC, current open_liability = 0, total bettor balances ~ 0. Two colluding (or merely simultaneous high-roller) bettors each submit a single bet whose potential_payout is 8,000 USDC at the same instant. Both placement transactions run evaluate() concurrently: each reads open_liability=0, computes 0 + 0 + 8000 <= 10000, accepts, inserts the ticket, and increments open_liability (now 16,000). Both legs win. The operator now owes 16,000 USDC against a 10,000 bank — a 6,000 USDC shortfall the solvency gate was designed to prevent. At scale (many bettors, automated clients) the breach can be arbitrarily large.
findings.recommendation: Serialize the bank-gate read+commit. Inside the placement tx, take a transaction-scoped advisory lock on the singleton bank-state before reading it (e.g. SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(<fixed bank key>)) OR SELECT ... FOR UPDATE the riskzilla_bank_state row at the top of evaluate() so concurrent placements serialize on it and each sees the prior increment. The advisory-lock approach (already used for nextPayoutRefID in settlement/store.go) avoids a hot-row hotspot vs. always FOR UPDATE-ing. Alternatively run the placement tx at SERIALIZABLE and retry on 40001 — but an explicit lock is cheaper and deterministic for a single hot row. The same lock will also close finding #2 (per-match cap) since both gates read from the same tx.

WHY SEVERITY IS OVERSTATED / NOT ATTACKER FUND-LOSS:

findings.title: Per-match / per-tier liability cap is bypassable under concurrent placements — bucket liability reads do not observe in-flight bets
findings.description: The per-(match, market, outcome) liability buckets used for the match-liability cap (line 569) are computed from a CTE over `tickets` filtered to `status IN ('accepted','pending_delay')` (line 370-371, 398-400) with plain SELECTs — no row locking and no advisory lock. Under READ COMMITTED, a placement transaction cannot see the rows another concurrent (uncommitted) placement is about to insert. The placement tx only holds a FOR UPDATE lock on the placing user's own users/wallets rows (service.ts line 320/332), which does NOT serialize placements by different users on the SAME match. So N simultaneous bets by different bettors on the same (match, market, outcome) each evaluate the bucket's liability_before from a snapshot missing all the other in-flight bets, each computes liability_after under the matchCap, and all are accepted — collectively breaching the per-tier match_liability_micro cap. (The per-BETTOR cap query is filtered to one user_id and that user's placements serialize on their own users-row lock, so the bettor cap is not exploitable by a single user; the exposed surface is the cross-user aggregate match cap.) Impact is bounded by how many bettors can hit the same hot outcome in the evaluate() window, but for a popular live market that window is exactly when correlated action arrives.
findings.exploitScenario: A tier-1 (tight cap) CS2 match has match_liability_micro = 500 USDC on the favourite. Five bettors each place a 200 USDC stake at 2.0 on the favourite within the same ~50ms window. Each placement's evaluate() reads the bucket with zero prior open payout (the other four are uncommitted), computes an incremental liability of ~200 well under the 500 cap, and accepts. The favourite wins; the operator pays out 5 x 400 = 2,000 USDC against a market it had capped at 500 — the liability ceiling that exists precisely to bound per-match exposure is silently exceeded.
findings.recommendation: Gate the liability evaluation behind a serializing lock keyed by match (or by the bank-state singleton as in finding #1). A transaction-scoped advisory lock on hashtext(matchId) taken at the start of the placement tx would force concurrent same-match placements to serialize so each sees the previously-committed bucket liability. If multiple matches are on a combo, lock them in a deterministic (sorted) order to avoid deadlock. Reusing a single bank-state advisory lock for the whole engine evaluation is the simplest fix and also resolves finding #1.

findings.title: open_liability_micro leaks when the bet-delay worker rejects a delayed ticket — placement increment is never reversed
findings.description: RiskzillaEngine.commitAccepted (services/api/src/lib/riskzilla/engine.ts line 629-635) increments riskzilla_bank_state.open_liability_micro by the ticket's full potential_payout for EVERY accepted placement, and it is called unconditionally for both 'accepted' and 'pending_delay' tickets (bets/service.ts line 1073 runs after the ticket insert regardless of delay). When a ticket goes to pending_delay and the bet-delay worker later REJECTS it (odds drift exceeded, market suspended, outcome inactive — worker.go evaluate() returns actionReject), store.RejectAndRefund (store.go line 328) sets status='rejected', unlocks the stake, and writes a bet_refund ledger row, but it does NOT decrement open_liability_micro. The decrement only ever happens in settlement (services/settlement/internal/store/store.go line 621, UpdateRiskzillaBankOnSettle), which runs exclusively for tickets that reach settle from status='accepted' (settler.go maybeSettleTicket gates on t.Status == 'accepted', line 564). A rejected ticket is never settled, so its placement-time liability contribution stays in open_liability_micro permanently. Confirmed by the recompute endpoint (admin/riskzilla/bank.ts line 322-328) which rebuilds open_liability from `tickets WHERE status IN ('accepted','pending_delay')` — i.e. it EXCLUDES 'rejected', proving the live counter and the canonical recompute disagree after any delayed-bet rejection. The drift is monotonic-upward (over-states liability), which biases the bank gate (finding #1) toward wrongly REJECTING legitimate future bets, and only an admin running /admin/riskzilla/bank/recompute clears it. The accept-with-updated-odds path (AcceptWithUpdatedOdds, store.go line 314-321) correctly adjusts by (new-old) delta, making the missing reject-path decrement clearly an omission rather than intended.

Each rejection leaks its potential payout into open_liability_micro. Over a session open_liability inflates well above the true sum of open tickets, pushing `userBalances + openLiability + newBet > bankLimit` true prematurely, so the operator starts rejecting valid bets with bank_limit_exceeded (lost revenue) until someone notices and runs recompute. A bettor who repeatedly submits delayed bets they expect to be drift-rejected could deliberately inflate the counter to deny service to other bettors on the same bank.
findings.recommendation: In RejectAndRefund, decrement open_liability_micro by the ticket's potential_payout_micro for USDC tickets in the same transaction, mirroring settlement's UpdateRiskzillaBankOnSettle (GREATEST(0, open_liability_micro - $payout)). Pass the potential payout (already on PendingTicket.PotentialPayoutMicro) into RejectAndRefund. Gate on currency=USDC to match the engine's RISKZILLA_CURRENCY fence so OZ-demo rejects don't touch the counter. Add a regression test that places a delayed USDC ticket, rejects it via the worker, and asserts open_liability_micro returns to its pre-placement value.

findings.title: deploy.sh sources the entire .env into the deploy shell, exposing HD_MASTER_MNEMONIC / JWT_SECRET / ODDIN_TOKEN via /proc/<pid>/environ during the deploy window
findings.description: When a deploy carries a pending migration, deploy.sh runs `set -a; . "${REPO_ROOT}/.env"; set +a` (lines 85-87) purely to obtain DATABASE_URL for the migrate step (line 90). `set -a` auto-exports every assignment while the file is sourced, so the entire .env — JWT_SECRET, REFRESH_COOKIE_SECRET, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, ODDIN_TOKEN, and the crown-jewel HD_MASTER_MNEMONIC (when set) — becomes an exported environment variable in the deploy process. `set +a` only stops further auto-export; it does NOT unset what was already exported. As a result every child process spawned for the remainder of the script — `pnpm db:migrate`, `docker compose build` (line 105), `docker compose up --force-recreate` (line 120), `make recreate-web` (line 126), `docker exec caddy validate` (line 144), and `smoke.sh` (line 157) — inherits the full secret set in its environment, readable from /proc/<pid>/environ for the entire build+recreate+smoke window (minutes on this box). This is precisely the anti-pattern the sibling scripts call out and deliberately avoid: dump-db.sh (lines 37-47) and pg_backup.sh (lines 6-12, 62-68) document "we do NOT `set -a; . .env` because that would dump JWT_SECRET + ODDIN_TOKEN + HD_MASTER_MNEMONIC into the environment where any concurrent process could read /proc/<pid>/environ" and instead grep out only the three postgres keys they need. deploy.sh needs only DATABASE_URL and uses the same broad source the others rejected.
findings.exploitScenario: During any migration-bearing `make deploy`, a second process running as the `team` user (or root) on the box — a compromised dev tool, a malicious dependency invoked by the parallel `docker compose build`, or any lateral foothold — reads /proc/<deploy-pid>/environ (or the environ of the build/recreate children) and exfiltrates HD_MASTER_MNEMONIC. With the master mnemonic the attacker can derive every on-chain deposit/withdrawal key and drain the operator's real USDC funds, completely bypassing the signer container's isolation, the 4-eyes withdrawal flow, and every API-layer control.
findings.recommendation: Replace the `set -a; . .env; set +a` block with a targeted read of just DATABASE_URL using the same `read_env_var` helper pattern the backup scripts already use (grep -E '^DATABASE_URL=' .env | head -1 | cut -d= -f2-), then `export DATABASE_URL="${DATABASE_URL//@postgres:/@127.0.0.1:}"`. This keeps the rest of the secret material out of the deploy shell and out of every child process's environ — closing the same /proc-readable window the operator already hardened the cron and pre-deploy-dump paths against. The entire signer-isolation architecture (separate container, tmpfs socket, os.Unsetenv at boot) exists to keep HD_MASTER_MNEMONIC out of readable process environments; deploy.sh briefly reintroduces it.

findings.title: ws-gateway accepts 100 MiB WebSocket frames (no maxPayload) in a 256 MiB container — anonymous single-frame OOM
findings.description: The WebSocketServer is created as `new WebSocketServer({ noServer: true })` (line 288) with NO `maxPayload` option, so the `ws` library default of 100 MiB per message applies. The message handler (line 385-392) does `raw.toString()` on every inbound frame before JSON.parse. The WS upgrade is explicitly anonymous-friendly (authenticate() is best-effort; a missing/invalid cookie still gets a connection per lines 331-358) and gated only by an Origin allowlist, which any non-browser client (or a malicious page that the user already has open on oddzilla.cc) can satisfy. The ws-gateway container is sized at `mem_limit: 256m` (documented in CLAUDE.md and referenced in the comment at line 87-88). A single ~100 MiB binary/text frame is buffered by ws, then `.toString()` doubles it to a ~200 MiB UTF-16 JS string — far over the 256 MiB cap — OOM-killing the container and dropping live odds + ticket frames for every connected bettor. A few concurrent frames make it deterministic. MAX_CLIENTS and MAX_SUBSCRIPTIONS_PER_CLIENT bound connection/subscription count but do nothing about per-frame size.
findings.exploitScenario: Attacker opens a WS to wss://oddzilla.cc/ws with Origin: https://oddzilla.cc (trivially set from a non-browser client, or from JS on any oddzilla.cc tab the victim already has open). No login needed. Sends a single 100 MiB text frame of JSON-ish junk. ws buffers it; the handler calls raw.toString() producing a ~200 MiB string; the 256 MiB container OOMs and is restarted by Docker. Repeating on each restart keeps live odds and ticket-settlement frames down for the whole site, and at scale the bet slip's WS-driven odds refresh stops working for all bettors.
findings.recommendation: Set an explicit small `maxPayload` on the WebSocketServer (e.g. `new WebSocketServer({ noServer: true, maxPayload: 16 * 1024 })`). The protocol's largest legitimate client frame is a subscribe envelope with up to MAX_SUBSCRIPTIONS_PER_CLIENT match ids — a few KiB. ws closes the connection with 1009 (message too big) automatically once maxPayload is set, before any buffer or toString allocation. Optionally also reject oversize before toString in the message handler as defense in depth.

findings.title: Self-service withdrawal endpoints have no rate limit and no max-pending cap — unbounded admin-queue / DB-lock flooding
findings.description: walletRoutes is registered in server.ts (line 230) with no group config, the global rate limiter is `global: false` (server.ts:158-162), and none of the wallet handlers declare a route-level `config.rateLimit`. POST /wallet/withdrawals (line 195), POST /wallet/addresses (line 336), DELETE /wallet/addresses/:id (line 380) and POST /wallet/withdrawals/:id/cancel (line 398) are therefore unlimited per authenticated user. There is also no cap on the number of open/'requested' withdrawals a user may hold (grep for pending/max-withdrawal guards returns nothing). Each POST /wallet/withdrawals opens a transaction, takes `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the user's USDC wallet row, inserts a withdrawals row, and inserts a wallet_ledger audit row. A user with any positive balance can spam this to mint thousands of tiny 'requested' withdrawal rows (each locking a sliver of balance), then loop POST /wallet/withdrawals/:id/cancel (also unlimited, also FOR UPDATE + ledger insert) to churn the lock and unlock balance, repeating indefinitely. This floods the operator's 4-eyes withdrawal queue and generates sustained write/lock load against a 10-connection API pool (packages/db/src/index.ts: max 10).
findings.exploitScenario: A logged-in bettor (real or a throwaway account funded with the 1000 OZ signup bonus — though OZ has no withdrawals, USDC requires a balance) with a small USDC balance scripts: loop { POST /wallet/withdrawals amountMicro=1 } until balance locked, then loop { POST /wallet/withdrawals/:id/cancel ; POST /wallet/withdrawals } forever. With no throttle this generates thousands of withdrawal rows and ledger rows per minute, buries the admin withdrawal review screen in noise, and contends on the wallet row lock + the 10-slot DB pool, degrading API latency for all users.

The cashout module already establishes the per-user keyGenerator pattern (services/api/src/modules/cashout/routes.ts:28-49) — reuse it.

findings.title: Anonymous /catalog/search and list endpoints have no rate limit and run leading-wildcard ILIKE scans that can exhaust the 10-connection DB pool
findings.description: Every /catalog/* route (server.ts:231) is anonymous and none declares a `config.rateLimit` (the global limiter is opt-in, server.ts:158). GET /catalog/search (line 1766) fires FOUR parallel queries via Promise.all, each using leading-wildcard ILIKE (`needle = '%' + escaped + '%'`, line 1777) on name/abbreviation/team columns — a leading `%` defeats any btree index, forcing sequential scans. Two of those queries also join matches→tournaments→categories→sports and include the `hasActiveMarket` EXISTS correlated subquery against the markets table (line 317-325), and the competitor query joins matches on `home OR away competitor id` (line 1856-1859, an OR-join). GET /catalog/matches (line 1511) and /catalog/sports/:slug similarly run the multi-join + hasActiveMarket EXISTS on every call. The API Postgres pool is capped at max:10 (packages/db/src/index.ts:9-12). Because there is no per-IP throttle on these endpoints, an unauthenticated attacker issuing concurrent /catalog/search requests (each holding a pool connection for the duration of 4 scan-heavy queries) can saturate all 10 connections, after which every other API request (auth, bets, wallet, settlement-adjacent reads) queues behind them.
findings.exploitScenario: An attacker with no account runs a small concurrency loop: for i in 1..50 in parallel { GET /catalog/search?q=<random 1-3 chars> }. Each request runs 4 sequential-scan ILIKE queries over competitors/matches with multi-table joins and the markets EXISTS subquery, each holding one of the 10 pool connections for hundreds of ms. Sustained, this keeps the pool fully occupied; legitimate bettor traffic (login, place bet, view wallet) blocks on connection acquisition and times out, taking the storefront effectively offline without any auth or large payloads.
findings.recommendation: Apply a per-IP rate limit to the catalog read routes (the community module already does exactly this — services/api/src/modules/community/routes.ts:96-98 uses 60/min for anonymous reads with the rationale 'a scraper can't paginate the entire feed in linear time'). At minimum gate /catalog/search tightly (e.g. 30/min/IP) since it is the most expensive anonymous endpoint. Consider trigram (pg_trgm GIN) indexes if leading-wildcard search must stay, so the scans become index-assisted rather than sequential.

findings.title: ws-gateway has no per-IP connection cap and no inbound message rate limit — single source can exhaust the global client cap and churn Redis
findings.description: Connection admission is governed solely by a GLOBAL cap `MAX_CLIENTS = 5000` (line 91, checked at line 337). There is no per-IP or per-user connection limit, and the upgrade explicitly accepts anonymous clients (line 331-358). A single attacker IP can therefore open up to 5000 connections and deny WebSocket service (live odds, ticket frames, chat) to every legitimate visitor — the cap that was added to prevent reconnect-storm OOM also makes it trivial for one host to monopolise all 5000 slots. Separately, the inbound message handler (line 385-409) has no rate limit: a connected client can send subscribe/unsubscribe envelopes in a tight loop. findings.title: Analysis/ticket inspiration counters can be self-inflated and sockpuppet-farmed (no self-action guard, no anti-sybil) — gameable Oz loyalty credit + leaderboard ranking
findings.description:
POST /community/copy/:communityTicketId increments two inspiration counters and can mint Oz loyalty credit, with no guard against the author/owner inflating their own content and no barrier to sockpuppet farming.

Concretely:
1. The community_ticket_inspirations bump (lines 547-566) and the analysis_inspirations bump (lines 590-622) dedup ONLY on (id, viewerUserId)/(analysisId, viewerId). There is NO check that `viewer.id !== ct.ownerId` (ticket owner, line 446) or `viewer.id !== analysisRow.authorId` (line 582). The author is a valid distinct viewer and can count toward their own inspiration_count.
2. When analyses.inspiration_count crosses 9->10 the engine credits the author Oz via creditEngagementFloor (routes.ts:616-621 -> analyses-rewards.ts:64-78), up to 250 Oz; and at 500 a flat +50 (routes.ts:627-631).
3. analyses.inspiration_count is the sort key for GET /community/analyses?sort=most_inspired (analyses.ts:891-893) and the V1 `recommended` ranker weights inspiration_count*2 (analyses.ts:303-315). community_tickets.inspiration_count is the sort key for the Best Wins `copied` feed.

There is no captcha, and email verification is only a dismissible banner (not a gate on bets/community actions), so spinning up N fresh accounts to copy/inspire a target analysis is trivial (signup is per-IP rate-limited 10/min but rotatable). An author can pin their own analysis to the top of the `most_inspired` / `recommended` surfaces and mint the engagement-floor + milestone Oz at will.

IMPACT IS LIMITED TO REPUTATION/RANKING, NOT FUNDS. The minted balance lands in oz_ledger/oz_balance_user, which migration 0076_oz_ledger.sql declares earn-only with no spend/redemption path; a codebase-wide search confirmed no debit/redeem/convert path exists, and oz_balance is never bridged to the USDC wallet or to withdrawals (wallet/routes.ts withdrawals hard-code currency='USDC'). So the concrete harm is (a) inflated standing on the public Top Authors / Most Inspired / Best Wins surfaces and (b) inflated cosmetic Oz totals — both of which mislead other bettors about who is a credible tipster (the product's entire premise) but cause no direct monetary loss today.

This becomes a real-money issue the moment the planned Oz redemption / spend flow lands (the migration explicitly anticipates 'the migration that introduces the first redemption path'). At that point the same self-farm becomes a mint-money primitive, so it should be fixed before redemption ships.
findings.exploitScenario: An analyst publishes an analysis attached to a tiny real-money ticket. They register 10 throwaway accounts (no email verification required to act; rotate source IP to dodge the 10/min signup limit), and from each call POST /community/copy/<ticketId>. The 10th distinct viewer pushes analyses.inspiration_count to exactly 10, firing creditEngagementFloor and crediting the author up to 250 Oz. The same 10 copies pin the analysis to the top of GET /community/analyses?sort=most_inspired and inflate the `recommended` feed score, making a low-skill author appear to be the community's most-followed tipster. Repeating across many analyses both farms the cosmetic Oz leaderboard and manufactures social proof that drives real bettors to copy the farmer's bets.
findings.recommendation: 1. Reject self-inspiration: in the copy handler, skip both counter bumps (and the engagement-floor / milestone credit) when viewer.id === ct.ownerId and when viewer.id === analysisRow.authorId. 2. Gate inspiration-driven Oz credit (and ideally any inspiration that counts toward ranking) on accounts that have cleared a real-cost signal — e.g. require users.email_verified_at IS NOT NULL for the viewer, and/or require the viewer to have actually placed the copied bet (a real stake) rather than merely hitting the copy endpoint, before the inspiration counts toward the engagement-floor threshold. 3. Before the Oz redemption/spend flow ships, treat inspiration-derived credits as Sybil-sensitive: add device/IP-cluster or velocity checks on the (analysis_id) inspiration accrual, since the same farm becomes a direct mint-money path once Oz has cash equivalence.

findings.title: Audit-log chain verifier exists but is never run automatically — tamper-evidence is dormant until a human SSHes in
findings.description: The SHA-256 hash-chain integrity verifier admin_audit_chain_check() is defined and correct, but it is NOT exposed through any API endpoint, cron job, sampler, or alert. The ONLY way it runs is a human operator manually executing a documented `ssh team@... docker exec ... psql -c "SELECT ... FROM admin_audit_chain_check()"` command (OPERATIONS.md:375, CLAUDE.md:498). There is no in-product surface (e.g. /admin/audit/integrity) and no scheduled check writing the result anywhere. Tamper-evidence that nobody ever evaluates provides no detection — a malicious DB-level edit would break the chain at every later row exactly as designed, yet remain unnoticed indefinitely because nothing compares stored row_hash to the recomputed value on any cadence. Confirmed: grep for `admin_audit_chain_check`/`chainCheck`/`verifyChain` across the whole repo returns only the migration, the schema comment, and docs — zero application call sites.
findings.exploitScenario: An attacker (or a rogue operator) with direct Postgres access mutates a historical admin_audit_log row — e.g. rewrites the `afterJson` of a `withdrawal.confirm` to hide a fraudulent payout, or changes `actor_user_id`. The chain breaks at that row and every subsequent row, but because no automated job ever calls admin_audit_chain_check(), the divergence is invisible until (and unless) an incident prompts someone to remember the manual SSH command. For a real-money sportsbook this means the tamper-evidence control is effectively off in steady state.
findings.recommendation: Wire admin_audit_chain_check() into an operational signal: (a) a daily cron (same crontab as the pg backup) that runs `SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT ok) FROM admin_audit_chain_check()` and pages/alerts on any non-zero result, and/or (b) an admin-only endpoint that returns the broken count so the monitoring page surfaces it alongside the other KPIs. Persist the last-checked head id + row count so the next finding (tail deletion) is also caught.
